step: Work Permit Pathway Assessment
deadline_label: Before departure — at least 12 weeks ahead for LMIA paths; 4 weeks minimum for LMIA-exempt IMP
non_obvious_official_guidance: Foreign nationals generally require a work permit to work in Canada. Permits fall into two categories: LMIA-based (requiring a positive Labour Market Impact Assessment from ESDC confirming no qualified Canadian was available) and LMIA-exempt under the International Mobility Program (IMP), covering intra-company transfers, CUSMA/USMCA professionals, significant benefit to Canada, and others. US and Mexican citizens may use CUSMA professional categories; EU nationals have no equivalent bilateral framework with Canada and require either LMIA or a qualifying IMP category.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Three critical traps: (1) 'LMIA-exempt' does not mean 'no employer compliance obligation' — IMP employers must submit an Offer of Employment through the IRCC Employer Portal and pay a C$230 Employer Compliance Fee per position before the employee can apply for a work permit, even for intra-company transfers; skipping this step invalidates the application. (2) CUSMA professionals must prove their occupation precisely matches Schedule I of CUSMA AND holds the specified credentials — a job title match alone is insufficient; CBSA officers at the port of entry make the final admissibility determination and can refuse. (3) Quebec-destined workers require a separate provincial Certificate of Acceptance (CAQ) from MIFI even for LMIA-exempt categories, adding 4–8 weeks to the timeline.
non_obvious_action_required: Classify the employee's nationality and job category before anything else. For IMP categories: register for the IRCC Employer Portal and submit the Offer of Employment to obtain a Job Offer Number before the employee applies. For LMIA paths: contact ESDC immediately — standard processing is 60+ business days; some positions require a 4-week National Job Bank advertisement run before filing. For Quebec-destined employees: initiate the CAQ and work permit applications in parallel, never sequentially.
source: IRCC – Do you need a work permit?

step: LMIA Application (Temporary Foreign Worker Program)
deadline_label: Minimum 12 weeks before desired start date — treat published averages as a floor
non_obvious_official_guidance: Employers hiring through the Temporary Foreign Worker Program must obtain a positive LMIA from ESDC confirming no qualified Canadian citizen or permanent resident was available for the role. Applications are submitted through the Employer Portal. The high-wage stream applies to positions above the provincial median hourly wage and requires a Transition Plan showing the employer's commitment to reducing reliance on temporary foreign workers.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The high-wage versus low-wage classification is based on the destination province's median hourly wage on the date of application — not the employer's own classification of the role. An incorrect stream assignment causes outright refusal. ESDC processing times published online are averages and routinely understate real delays; non-agricultural LMIA processing averaged 3–5 months in 2023–2024. Employers registering for the Employer Portal for the first time face a 5–10 business day account verification step that is not prominently disclosed. The Transition Plan must describe concrete workforce localisation steps; vague or boilerplate language is rejected.
non_obvious_action_required: Confirm the destination province's current median hourly wage on the exact date of filing — not the offer date. Register for the ESDC Employer Portal at least two weeks before the intended filing date to absorb the verification delay. Budget 12–16 weeks minimum for the complete LMIA process; treat the published average as a floor, not a ceiling. Do not issue any fixed-start-date offer letter to the employee until a positive LMIA is confirmed in writing from ESDC.
source: ESDC – Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA)

step: Employer Offer of Employment Submission via IRCC Employer Portal (IMP)
deadline_label: Before employee submits work permit application — allow 5–10 days for portal registration
non_obvious_official_guidance: Under the International Mobility Program, employers who hire LMIA-exempt workers must submit an Offer of Employment electronically through the IRCC Employer Portal and pay the C$230 Employer Compliance Fee before the employee can apply for a work permit. The resulting Job Offer Number is a mandatory field in the employee's work permit application.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Many HR teams treat 'LMIA-exempt' as equivalent to 'no employer administration' — this is incorrect. The work permit application will be refused or flagged at the port of entry if no valid Offer of Employment is on file in the IRCC system. The Employer Portal requires a GCKey or Sign-In Partner account; first-time employer registrations must allow 5–10 business days for identity verification — a step not prominently disclosed. For Intra-Company Transfer roles claiming 'specialised knowledge': CBSA frequently challenges this category; a generic expertise description does not qualify — the employee's knowledge must be proprietary, company-specific, and demonstrably not available from the Canadian labour market.
non_obvious_action_required: Register for the IRCC Employer Portal as soon as the hire decision is made, not close to the travel date. Submit the Offer of Employment and pay the C$230 fee before sending the employee any application package. Pass the Job Offer Number to the employee — it is a required field. For ICT Specialised Knowledge roles: prepare a detailed position description that maps the employee's knowledge to the legal definition explicitly; retain org charts and financial statements demonstrating the corporate relationship for potential CBSA review at the port of entry.
source: IRCC – Employer Portal: Offer of Employment

step: Quebec Certificate of Acceptance (CAQ) — Quebec-Destined Employees Only
authority: Ministère de l'Immigration, de la Francisation et de l'Intégration (MIFI)
deadline_label: Initiate at least 8 weeks before work permit application submission
non_obvious_official_guidance: All foreign workers taking up employment in Quebec require both a federal work permit and a provincial Certificate of Acceptance (CAQ) issued by MIFI, unless they fall into a specific CAQ-exempt category such as CUSMA professionals, certain diplomatic postings, or some short-duration categories. Processing is entirely separate from and independent of federal work permit processing.
non_obvious_actual_reality: HR teams managing multi-province deployments routinely overlook the CAQ for Quebec assignments, treating federal LMIA-exempt clearance as sufficient. A valid federal work permit without a valid CAQ does not authorise work in Quebec — the employee is in violation of Quebec immigration law from day one. MIFI processing times are not visible in IRCC's processing time tools and have ranged from 4–10 weeks in 2023–2024. Transfers of employees already working elsewhere in Canada (e.g., Toronto to Montreal) may not require a new federal work permit if their permit conditions allow it, but DO require a new CAQ for Quebec employment — this is almost universally overlooked.
non_obvious_action_required: For any role in Quebec: initiate the CAQ application on monportail.immigration-quebec.gouv.qc.ca in parallel with the federal step — never sequentially. Verify whether the employee's specific permit category is CAQ-exempt before filing to avoid unnecessary applications. Budget 6–10 weeks for MIFI processing using the conservative end. The employee must carry both the federal work permit and the CAQ certificate. For employees transferring from another Canadian province to Quebec: confirm whether a new CAQ is required even if the federal permit is not changing.
source: MIFI – Certificate of Acceptance of Quebec (CAQ) for Temporary Workers

step: Interim Private Health Insurance During Provincial Wait Period
authority: Private Insurer (employer-arranged); Provincial Health Ministry (wait period governance)
deadline_label: Arrange before employee departs home country
non_obvious_official_guidance: Provincial and territorial health insurance plans are free to eligible residents but most provinces impose a waiting period before coverage activates. Ontario imposes a 3-month wait; British Columbia imposes a 3-month wait; Quebec imposes a wait for certain permit categories; Alberta eliminated its waiting period in 2009. During the wait, any medical costs are borne fully by the employee unless privately covered.
non_obvious_actual_reality: A single Canadian emergency department visit costs C$800–2,000+ without insurance; specialist or surgical costs are far higher. Employees from countries with universal health access (France, Germany, Nordic states) are systematically unprepared for this gap. Provincial health card issuance does not equal coverage activation — Ontario mails the OHIP card ahead of the activation date, creating a false sense of security when the card is presented and the claim is rejected. Employer relocation packages that do not explicitly include interim health coverage expose the company to employee grievances and reimbursement demands when surprise medical bills arrive.
non_obvious_action_required: Arrange employer-sponsored expatriate or travel health insurance to cover the first three months before the employee departs their home country. Confirm the exact wait period for the destination province — Alberta has none; Ontario and BC impose 3 months; others vary. Explicitly brief the employee in writing that their provincial health card, once issued, is not active until the wait period expires. Do not rely on the employee's home-country health insurer — most policies terminate on emigration or cap overseas emergency coverage at 30–90 days.
source: Government of Canada – Provincial and Territorial Health Insurance Plans

step: Port of Entry — Work Permit Issuance by CBSA
field_label: Work Permit — CBSA Issuance at POE
deadline_label: On arrival — present complete documentation at primary inspection
non_obvious_official_guidance: Many work permit categories — including CUSMA professionals, ICT under IMP, and open work permits for spouses of skilled workers — are issued at the port of entry rather than at a Canadian visa office abroad. The employee presents documentation to a CBSA officer who makes the final admissibility determination and prints the permit. An approved eTA for visa-exempt nationals does not guarantee admission or the specific permit conditions requested.
non_obvious_actual_reality: CBSA officers at the POE have full discretion to refuse admission, change the occupation category, restrict the employer, or issue a shorter permit validity than requested — even when all documentation appears complete. CUSMA refusals most commonly occur when the occupation does not precisely match Schedule I of CUSMA, or when credentials presented are PDF copies rather than original notarised documents. Pre-clearance at US airports with Canadian preclearance facilities (e.g., Toronto Pearson, Vancouver) means the admissibility decision is made on US soil — a refusal results in being turned back before entering Canada, creating an immediate return-travel situation.
non_obvious_action_required: Prepare a complete POE documentation package: employer offer letter on company letterhead (specifying job title, CUSMA category reference or IMP Job Offer Number, salary, and duration), educational credentials as originals or lawyer-certified copies with certified translation, valid passport, eTA or visa confirmation, and any LMIA or IMP Job Offer Number printout. Brief the employee to declare the correct purpose of entry — 'to work' not 'to visit'. Have an immigration counsel's phone number available for use during a prolonged secondary inspection. Do not rely on documents stored on a phone — CBSA expects printed originals or certified paper copies.
source: CBSA – Working in Canada Temporarily

step: Social Insurance Number (SIN) Application at Service Canada
authority: Service Canada (Employment and Social Development Canada)
form_name: SIN Application (in-person; no advance form required)
deadline_label: Before first day of work — legally required before payroll can be processed
non_obvious_official_guidance: A Social Insurance Number is required to work legally in Canada, file taxes, and access federal government programs. Foreign nationals with a valid work permit apply in person at any Service Canada office. Work permit holders receive a SIN beginning with '9', valid for the duration of the work permit only.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Three non-obvious realities: (1) The '9' SIN prefix is visible to any institution that queries the ESDC system — some private landlords and smaller financial institutions flag it as a risk indicator, creating friction when opening bank accounts or signing leases, even though the number is fully valid. (2) The SIN must be provided to the employer's payroll department before the first payroll run — employees who delay to 'settle in first' cause payroll holds and delayed first pay. (3) Service Canada offices in city-centre locations (Toronto downtown, Vancouver downtown) have 60–90 minute wait times during morning hours in September and January; suburban locations have significantly shorter queues.
non_obvious_action_required: Apply for the SIN within the first 1–2 business days of arrival — before finding permanent accommodation if needed, as no permanent address is required. Bring the valid work permit and passport only; no other documents are required for foreign nationals. Choose a suburban Service Canada location over downtown to avoid queues. Provide the SIN to the employer's payroll department the same day — do not wait for a payslip. Remind the employee that the SIN is confidential and that businesses or landlords who request it for purposes other than payroll or banking are likely acting outside their authority under PIPEDA.
source: Service Canada – Apply for a Social Insurance Number (SIN)

step: Provincial Health Card Enrollment
authority: Provincial Health Ministry (ServiceOntario / Health Insurance BC / RAMQ / Alberta Health / others)
deadline_label: Day 1–3 of arrival — enrol immediately to start the mandatory wait-period clock
non_obvious_official_guidance: Each province administers its own public health insurance plan. Work permit holders with a permit of sufficient duration are eligible to enrol. Most provinces impose a wait before coverage activates: Ontario (OHIP) — 3 months; British Columbia (MSP via Health Insurance BC) — 3 months; Quebec (RAMQ) — 3 months for permit holders of 6+ months duration; Alberta — no waiting period; Nova Scotia — 3 months; Manitoba — 3 months.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The wait-period clock starts from the date the province registers the resident — not the date of physical arrival. An employee who waits a week to register loses a week of the countdown to coverage. BC's health insurance is administered by Health Insurance BC (HIBC), a separate body with a distinct online portal — employees searching generically for 'BC health card' commonly land on provincial pages that do not link to the correct HIBC application path. Ontario OHIP cards are mailed to the address on file; if the address changes during the wait period and is not updated with ServiceOntario, the card goes to the wrong address and the employee discovers the problem only at a medical appointment.
non_obvious_action_required: Enrol in the provincial health plan within the first 3 days of arrival, even using a temporary address such as a hotel or employer-arranged accommodation — most provinces accept this. For Ontario: attend a ServiceOntario location in person with the work permit, passport, and proof of Ontario address. For BC: apply online via hibc.gov.bc.ca with the work permit and passport details. For Quebec: apply to RAMQ at ramq.gouv.qc.ca; confirm eligibility based on permit category and duration. Update the address with the health authority as soon as a permanent address is confirmed.
source: Health Canada – Provincial and Territorial Health Insurance Plans

step: Canadian Bank Account Opening
deadline_label: Within first week — required for payroll direct deposit and rental deposits
non_obvious_official_guidance: Under federal financial consumer protection regulations, Canadian banks must open a basic personal bank account for any individual who presents acceptable government-issued identification. Foreign nationals can open accounts with a valid passport and work permit. A Social Insurance Number is not required to open the account, though banks request it for tax reporting purposes once obtained.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Despite the regulatory obligation, front-line bank staff frequently insist on a SIN as a mandatory prerequisite — this is incorrect under FCAC's Access to Basic Banking Services regulations. The refusal must be escalated to a branch manager by citing the FCAC right. The '9' SIN prefix triggers enhanced compliance review at some major institutions, extending approval by 3–5 business days after the SIN is provided. Credit history is not portable from the employee's home country; even a high-income employee starts with no Canadian credit bureau presence, limiting initial credit card limits, auto-leasing options, and rental applications — some landlords require a 3–6 month deposit in lieu of a credit check for new arrivals.
non_obvious_action_required: Open the bank account on day 1–2 of arrival — before or simultaneously with the SIN application. Bring passport plus work permit as the two-document identification set. If branch staff refuse without a SIN, invoke the FCAC Access to Basic Banking regulations and request the branch manager. After obtaining the SIN, add it to the bank account within 90 days as required for T5 interest income tax reporting. Provide the bank's transit number, institution number, and account number to employer payroll immediately for direct deposit setup.
source: FCAC – Opening a Bank Account in Canada

step: Canadian Tax Residency Determination
deadline_label: Determine before first payroll run — affects employer withholding from day one
non_obvious_official_guidance: Canada taxes residents on worldwide income and non-residents only on Canadian-source income. Residency is determined primarily by residential ties — a home in Canada, a spouse or dependants in Canada, personal property and social ties — not solely by days spent in the country. Part-year residents arriving mid-year are taxable on worldwide income from the date of entry only. CRA Form NR73 can be filed to obtain a formal determination, though it is optional and takes 5–6 months.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Canada's residential-ties test has no single bright-line rule, unlike the UK's Statutory Residence Test or France's 183-day threshold. The 'sojourner' rule can deem a person Canadian-resident after 183 calendar days even without residential ties — and the residential-ties analysis can apply simultaneously, creating dual-residency risk with treaty tie-breaker implications. A work permit holder who maintains a home and dependent family in their origin country while working in Canada may be a non-resident for tax purposes even after 183 days — but an employer that defaults to resident withholding without confirming residential ties creates a refund claim process that takes 12–18 months to resolve. Home-country departure tax obligations may also be triggered on the date of Canadian arrival.
non_obvious_action_required: Brief a Canadian tax advisor before the employee's first payroll run. If non-resident status is likely: the employer must withhold at the non-resident flat rate (25% or reduced treaty rate) under Part XIII tax, not standard TD1-based payroll deductions. Retain documentation of the employee's departure from the home country (lease termination, bank closures, school deregistration) to support the immigration date and break of home-country residence. Check the applicable Canada–[home country] tax treaty for residency tie-breaker provisions and treaty-reduced withholding rates.
source: CRA – Determining your residency status

step: TD1 Federal and Provincial Tax Declaration
form_name: TD1 (Federal) + TD1[Province] (e.g., TD1ON, TD1BC); TP-1015.3-V for Quebec provincial
deadline_label: On commencement of employment — or within 7 days of any claim change
non_obvious_official_guidance: All employees must complete a federal TD1 Personal Tax Credits Return and a provincial TD1 for the province of employment on commencement of work. These forms determine the personal tax credits the employer uses when calculating income tax to withhold from each pay cheque. Separate forms exist for each province and territory.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Two non-obvious traps: (1) Quebec is entirely different — Quebec administers its own provincial income tax separately; employees in Quebec complete the TP-1015.3-V for provincial and the standard federal TD1 for federal. Using any generic or Ontario-labelled provincial TD1 for a Quebec employee causes incorrect provincial withholding and is a common payroll-system misconfiguration. (2) Part-year residents who arrived after January 1 must prorate the basic personal amount for the number of days of Canadian residency in the calendar year — overclaiming the full annual amount results in a tax balance owing at the April 30 filing deadline, which surprises employees who assumed payroll was calibrated correctly.
non_obvious_action_required: Have both the federal TD1 and the correct provincial TD1 ready for the employee's first day. For Quebec: configure payroll to use the TP-1015.3-V for provincial withholding — verify the payroll system is not defaulting to a generic provincial TD1. Walk any employee arriving after January 1 through the basic personal amount proration: divide the full annual amount by 365 and multiply by the remaining days of the calendar year. Retain signed TD1 forms in the payroll file — they are required documentation in a CRA payroll audit.
source: CRA – TD1 Personal Tax Credits Returns

step: CPP/QPP Enrollment and Social Security Totalization Check
form_name: Certificate of Coverage (issued by home-country authority, if applicable)
deadline_label: From first pay period — no grace period or minimum duration exemption
non_obvious_official_guidance: All Canadian employees and employers must contribute to the Canada Pension Plan (CPP) — or, for Quebec employees, the Quebec Pension Plan (QPP) administered by Retraite Québec — from the first pay period regardless of immigration status or assignment length. Contribution rates and the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings are updated annually by CRA.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Work permit holders are subject to CPP/QPP contributions even on short assignments — there is no minimum duration threshold. The critical exception: Canada has bilateral social security totalization agreements with approximately 60 countries including most EU states, the UK, the US, and Australia. Employees covered by an agreement who hold a valid Certificate of Coverage from their home-country social security authority are exempt from CPP and may continue contributing solely to their home plan. Employers that do not check totalization treaty status inadvertently enrol an exempt employee in CPP while home-country contributions continue — correcting double-payment requires refund claims in both countries and typically takes 18–24 months. Quebec's QPP is a separate system; payroll not specifically configured for Quebec routes contributions to CPP instead, creating a distinct compliance failure.
non_obvious_action_required: Before the first payroll: verify whether Canada has a totalization agreement with the employee's home country using the ESDC agreement list. If yes: request the Certificate of Coverage from the home-country social security authority before the first pay period and do not begin CPP deductions until confirmed. If no agreement exists: enrol in CPP from day one. For Quebec employees: ensure payroll remits to Retraite Québec (QPP) — a different remittance account from CRA — and verify the system configuration explicitly.
source: ESDC – Canada's International Social Security Agreements

step: CRA My Account Registration
deadline_label: Within first month — required for online tax correspondence and benefit claims
source: CRA – My Account for Individuals

step: Address Registration Across Federal and Provincial Authorities
authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA); Provincial Health Ministry; Service Canada; Provincial Motor Vehicle Authority
deadline_label: Within 30 days of establishing permanent address; driver's licence exchange within 60–90 days (province-specific)
non_obvious_official_guidance: Canada has no central mandatory population registration system equivalent to Germany's Einwohnermeldeamt or France's mairie registration. Residents must separately update their address with CRA (for tax correspondence and benefits), the provincial health authority (for health card correspondence), Service Canada (for SIN and EI records), and the provincial motor vehicle authority (for driver's licence exchange deadline compliance).
non_obvious_actual_reality: Employees from countries with central registration (Germany, France, Norway, Sweden) assume a single registration satisfies all obligations — in Canada it does not. Missing CRA address updates means Notices of Assessment, GST/HST credit payments, and RRSP contribution room statements go to the wrong address; these are not automatically re-sent and are not accessible online until CRA My Account is activated and linked. Driver's licence exchange deadlines (Ontario: 60 days; BC: 90 days; Quebec: 90 days from becoming provincial resident) are inconsistently enforced but can void auto insurance collision coverage at the time of a claim — a risk rarely disclosed by insurers at policy inception.
non_obvious_action_required: Update address with CRA via My Account or by calling 1-800-959-8281 within 30 days of establishing a permanent address. Submit a provincial health card address update simultaneously — this also ensures the wait-period activation notice and renewed card reach the correct address. Register with the provincial motor vehicle authority and initiate the driver's licence exchange within the province-specific deadline. Confirm that payroll reflects the correct province of employment address — an incorrect province coding causes wrong provincial income tax withholding and affects T4 year-end reporting.
source: CRA – Change your address

step: Foreign Driver's Licence Exchange
authority: Provincial Ministry of Transportation / Motor Vehicle Authority (DriveTest Ontario; ICBC BC; SAAQ Quebec)
deadline_label: Within 60–90 days of becoming a provincial resident (province-specific)
non_obvious_official_guidance: Each province has its own rules for exchanging a foreign driver's licence for a provincial one. Some provinces have reciprocal agreements with specific countries permitting direct exchange without a road test; others require knowledge and/or road tests. A foreign licence may be used for a limited period after establishing provincial residency.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Reciprocity varies by province and origin country: Ontario recognises licences from Germany, France, Switzerland, Austria, Japan, and South Korea for direct exchange; BC does not recognise all the same countries as Ontario. An employee who drove lawfully under a foreign licence in one province and moves interprovincially faces the destination province's separate reciprocity rules. Auto insurance in Canada can be voided for collision claims if the insured was past the exchange deadline — this exposure is rarely disclosed by brokers at policy inception. DriveTest (Ontario) and ICBC (BC) appointment availability runs 3–8 weeks; without early booking, the deadline passes before the appointment is available.
non_obvious_action_required: On arrival, immediately look up the destination province's reciprocity list for the employee's home-country licence — do not assume recognition. Book the licence exchange appointment in the first week to absorb the wait time. If the home country is not on the reciprocal list: the employee must pass the written knowledge test and a road test, adding 2–4 months including wait times. Alert the employer fleet or travel insurance administrator if the employee will use a company vehicle before completing the exchange.
source: DriveTest Ontario – Exchange a Foreign Driver's Licence

step: Annual Income Tax Filing (T1 General Return)
form_name: T1 General — Income Tax and Benefit Return
deadline_label: April 30 annually (June 15 for self-employed); balance owing always due April 30
non_obvious_official_guidance: All Canadian tax residents must file a T1 General Return by April 30 reporting worldwide income earned during the period of Canadian tax residency. Non-residents who earned Canadian-source income also have filing obligations. The employer issues a T4 slip by the last day of February for the prior calendar year summarising employment income and deductions.
non_obvious_actual_reality: First-year filers face three non-obvious complications: (1) Part-year residency — standard CRA-certified NETFILE software does not automatically detect part-year residency and pre-fills fields on a full-year basis; failing to adjust for the arrival date results in overclaimed personal tax credits and a CRA review. (2) T1135 Foreign Income Verification — any employee who held foreign assets with a total cost base over C$100,000 at any point during the year must file a T1135; this includes foreign bank accounts, investment portfolios, and real property held abroad. Non-compliance attracts C$25/day penalties up to C$2,500/year plus potential gross negligence penalties. (3) Treaty elections — employees from treaty countries may claim treaty benefits to reduce effective Canadian tax on certain income types, but the required election forms (e.g., NR301) are almost universally missed by first-year filers without professional guidance.
non_obvious_action_required: Engage a Canadian tax professional for the first-year return to handle the part-year residency proration, T1135 assessment, and applicable treaty election forms. Collect all foreign income documentation (payslips, interest statements, foreign tax returns) for months before arrival — worldwide income in the arrival year is required for full annual disclosure even if not ultimately taxable in Canada. Calendar the T4 receipt deadline (end of February) and the April 30 filing deadline. Flag the T1135 obligation to the employee at the assignment start if they hold foreign assets exceeding C$100,000.
source: CRA – T1 General Income Tax and Benefit Return

step: Work Permit Renewal
form_name: IMM 1295 – Application to Change Conditions, Extend My Stay or Remain in Canada as a Worker
deadline_label: Apply at least 90–120 days before expiry; must file BEFORE expiry to maintain implied status
non_obvious_official_guidance: Work permit holders must renew before their current permit expires. A renewal application submitted before expiry confers 'implied status' — the right to continue working for the same employer under the same conditions while the renewal is pending. An application submitted even one day after expiry results in loss of status and a violation of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.
non_obvious_actual_reality: IRCC in-Canada work permit renewal processing times ranged from 60 to 180+ days in 2023–2024. Implied status is extinguished by a single day's lapse past permit expiry — there is no grace period. The '9' SIN expires on the same date as the work permit; once the renewed permit is issued, the employee must attend a Service Canada office to obtain an updated '9' SIN reflecting the new expiry date — a step that introduces payroll interruption risk if not managed proactively. For LMIA-based permits: a new positive LMIA is typically required for renewal unless specific bridging provisions apply, adding a further 3–5 months to the timeline.
non_obvious_action_required: Set HRIS alerts for 120 days before every work permit expiry date — 90 days is the regulatory floor but not a practical safe margin given current backlogs. File the renewal with complete supporting documents no later than 90 days before expiry; retain the IRCC submission acknowledgement as proof of implied status. Upon receiving the renewed permit: (1) update the HRIS record, (2) have the employee attend a Service Canada office immediately to obtain the updated '9' SIN, (3) initiate the provincial health card renewal in the same week.
source: IRCC – Extend your stay in Canada as a worker

step: Employment Insurance (EI) Contribution and Benefit Eligibility Awareness
authority: Service Canada (Employment and Social Development Canada)
deadline_label: Ongoing — premiums mandatory from first pay period; benefit eligibility conditional on permit status at time of claim
non_obvious_official_guidance: Employment Insurance premiums are mandatory for all employees and employers in Canada regardless of immigration status. Work permit holders accumulate insurable hours from their first day of employment. To claim EI benefits, the worker must have accumulated the required insurable hours (420–700 hours depending on the regional unemployment rate) AND hold valid Canadian work authorisation at the time of the claim.
non_obvious_actual_reality: A work permit holder whose permit expires during a period of unemployment cannot make an EI benefits claim — the right to work has lapsed, extinguishing claim eligibility for the gap. An employee can contribute premiums throughout a full 2-year assignment and then be unable to access benefits if the permit is not renewed before or at the same time as job loss. Employees do not typically realise that EI premium withholding (approximately 1.66% of insurable earnings in 2024) is mandatory even though their benefit access is conditional on permit status. Some bilateral totalization agreements include EI-equivalent provisions — but this is a separate check from the CPP exemption and must be verified independently.
non_obvious_action_required: Brief the employee explicitly at assignment start that EI benefit access requires valid work authorisation at the moment of any claim — a permit lapse extinguishes eligibility for the gap period even if premiums were paid. Plan permit renewals to ensure no lapse in work authorisation, particularly if layoff risk exists near the permit end date. For employees from countries with totalization agreements: verify separately whether the agreement covers EI equivalents — this is not automatic from a CPP exemption determination.
source: Service Canada – EI for foreign nationals working in Canada

step: Provincial Health Card Renewal on Work Permit Renewal
authority: Provincial Health Ministry (ServiceOntario / Health Insurance BC / RAMQ / others)
deadline_label: Immediately upon receipt of renewed work permit — do not wait for card expiry notice
non_obvious_official_guidance: Provincial health cards issued to work permit holders are tied to the permit validity period. When a work permit is renewed, the health card must be separately renewed with the provincial health authority to reflect the new permit end date. This is not automatic.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Employees who renew their work permit and assume health coverage continues uninterrupted are wrong — the health card expiry is not automatically extended. The lapse is discovered only when coverage is denied at a clinic, pharmacy, or hospital, often in a stressful or urgent situation. Ontario OHIP card renewal requires an in-person ServiceOntario visit and cannot be completed online; without proactive scheduling, the appointment wait can mean days of coverage gap. Some pharmacies and walk-in clinics will not process a drug claim against an expired health card, requiring the employee to pay out-of-pocket and file for reimbursement afterward.
non_obvious_action_required: Add provincial health card renewal as an explicit step on the work permit renewal checklist — it is a separate action, not a follow-on. For Ontario OHIP: attend a ServiceOntario location with the renewed work permit and the current (or expired) OHIP card. For BC MSP: update online via hibc.gov.bc.ca by uploading the renewed permit details. For Quebec RAMQ: submit updated permit details through the RAMQ online portal or by contacting RAMQ directly. Set a calendar alert 60 days before work permit expiry to trigger both the permit renewal process and the health card renewal simultaneously.
source: Ontario – Apply for OHIP and get a health card

step: Permanent Residency Pathway — Express Entry and Provincial Nominee Programs
authority: Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) / Provincial Nominee Program (PNP) authorities; MIFI (Quebec)
deadline_label: Create Express Entry profile as early as possible after commencing work — CRS points accrue from profile creation, not retroactively
non_obvious_official_guidance: Canada's primary managed economic immigration pathway is Express Entry, which uses a Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score to rank candidates for Invitations to Apply (ITAs) for permanent residence. Candidates with Canadian work experience typically qualify for the Canadian Experience Class (CEC) after 12 months of skilled work. Provincial Nominee Programs award 600 additional CRS points via a nomination, substantially accelerating the timeline. Quebec manages its own provincial immigration system through MIFI and is not covered by federal Express Entry draws.
non_obvious_actual_reality: CRS cut-off scores fluctuate significantly — scores ranged from 431 to 517 across 2023 draws, making profile timing material to candidacy. An employee who waits until work permit renewal pressure mounts to create an Express Entry profile loses months of CRS Canadian work experience points that would have accrued from the profile creation date. Some provincial PNP streams require employer endorsement (a supporting letter or job offer registered in the PNP system) — HR teams that do not proactively flag employer-supported streams leave the employee to discover them independently, typically too late. For Quebec employees: Express Entry draws do not apply; the MIFI Quebec Skilled Worker program is the primary pathway, and it operates on different criteria and quotas.
non_obvious_action_required: Brief the employee to create an Express Entry profile as early as possible after commencing work — do not wait for the permit renewal cycle. Review the destination province's PNP streams for employer-supported or sector-specific categories and confirm whether HR action (an endorsement letter or registered job offer) is needed. For Quebec employees: direct them to the MIFI immigration portal at immigration-quebec.gouv.qc.ca — the federal Express Entry system does not produce ITAs for Quebec. Monitor IRCC CRS draw results monthly to track when the employee's score becomes competitive for an ITA.
source: IRCC – Express Entry: Who can apply
